questions.q: Why does this lesson say "we'll know it if we see it" fails as a rollback trigger?
options: Because it is technically impossible to observe a failed migration
Because it isn't specific or measurable, making it a recipe for disagreement during the worst possible moment to have one
Because rollback triggers can only be defined by Salesforce Support
Because it would require a Full sandbox to evaluate
questions.explain: A real rollback trigger has to be specific and measurable, decided calmly during planning — a vague 'we'll know it' standard invites exactly the kind of high-pressure disagreement this lesson warns against.

questions.q: When is restoring from a pre-cutover backup described as the cleanest rollback mechanic?
options: Only after users have already created significant new data in the target org
Only when Hard Delete permission has not been granted
Only for phased migrations, never big-bang ones
If the rollback decision happens quickly, before much else has changed in the target org since cutover
questions.explain: A full backup restore undoes everything in one action, which is cleanest when little else has changed in the org yet — the more time passes and the more new activity accumulates, the less practical this option becomes.

questions.q: Why does Hard Delete matter specifically for some rollback scenarios?
options: Because Hard Delete is required for every single rollback, with no exceptions
Because Hard Delete automatically restores a pre-cutover backup

Because a true, permanent removal of migrated records (not just sending them to the Recycle Bin) requires the separate "Bulk API Hard Delete" permission, which should be granted before cutover, not during an emergency
Because Hard Delete is the only way to identify which records a migration job created
questions.explain: When rollback needs records truly, permanently gone rather than just sent to the Recycle Bin, Hard Delete is required — and it needs its own permission granted ahead of time, not requested for the first time mid-emergency.

questions.q: What is the "point of no return" in migration rollback planning?
options: The point past which a clean, complete rollback risks destroying real new business data created in the target org since cutover
The moment a cutover runbook is finalized
The exact midpoint of the freeze window
The moment Bulk API 2.0 issues a job Id
questions.explain: Once users have created genuinely new data in the target org, deleting 'everything this migration loaded' risks also destroying that new, unrelated data — which is why rollback can't be assumed to stay available indefinitely.

questions.q: Besides a full rollback, what does this lesson say contingency planning should also cover?
options: Nothing else — rollback is the only contingency worth planning for
Smaller, more survivable failure scenarios, like one object running long or a fixable subset of validation failures, that don't require undoing the whole migration
Only scenarios involving Hard Delete specifically
Only scenarios that occur during the rehearsal phase, never during actual cutover
questions.explain: Contingency planning should name smaller, more survivable scenarios and their planned responses in advance too, turning cutover day into executing pre-agreed responses rather than improvising under pressure.
